before: For American options the problem is harder than for European ones, since the early-exercise boundary is unknown and no closed form exists \cite{merton1973theory,hull2022options}.
after: An American contract adds a second difficulty. Its holder can exercise early, the exercise boundary has to be found as part of the solution, and no closed-form price exists \cite{merton1973theory,hull2022options}.

before: Lattice and simulation methods give accurate references \cite{cox1979option,longstaff2001valuing}, but they do not say how wrong a fast surrogate is at a new point.
after: Trees and Monte Carlo produce accurate reference values \cite{cox1979option,longstaff2001valuing}. They cannot tell us, however, the error of a fast surrogate at an unseen point.

before: \emph{Classical pricing.} The Black-Scholes model \cite{black1973pricing} and Merton's rational bounds \cite{merton1973theory} give the European price and the no-arbitrage conditions we test.
after: \emph{Reference pricers.} Our European ground truth is the closed-form price of \cite{black1973pricing}. The no-arbitrage conditions we test come from Merton's bounds \cite{merton1973theory}.

before: The binomial lattice of Cox, Ross and Rubinstein \cite{cox1979option} handles early exercise and serves here as the American reference.
after: For the American put we use the recombining tree of \cite{cox1979option}, which compares holding and exercising at every node.

before: Barone-Adesi and Whaley \cite{baroneadesi1987efficient} give a fast analytic approximation, and Longstaff and Schwartz \cite{longstaff2001valuing} price American options by least-squares Monte Carlo.
after: Two other routes exist: a quadratic analytic approximation \cite{baroneadesi1987efficient}, and simulation in which a regression estimates the value of continuing \cite{longstaff2001valuing}.

before: Stochastic volatility models \cite{heston1993closed} are usually solved with finite differences, for example ADI schemes \cite{inthout2010adi}. Textbook treatments of parity and early exercise are in \cite{hull2022options}.
after: Under stochastic volatility \cite{heston1993closed}, grid methods such as ADI splitting \cite{inthout2010adi} are a common choice. Standard texts such as \cite{hull2022options} cover put-call parity and early exercise.

before: \emph{Neural PDE solvers.} PINNs train a network so that a PDE residual, boundary terms and an initial or terminal term are small at sampled points \cite{raissi2019physics}. The Deep Galerkin Method \cite{sirignano2018dgm} follows a similar mesh-free idea and includes an American option example, and the deep BSDE method \cite{han2018solving} targets high-dimensional PDEs. Applied work has used PINNs for Black-Scholes type equations \cite{bai2022application}, for American options \cite{gatta2023meshless} and for the Heston model \cite{hainaut2024option}. To our knowledge, these studies focus on point accuracy rather than on calibrated error bands.
after: \emph{Networks as PDE solvers.} A PINN \cite{raissi2019physics} is fitted by penalising, at random points, how far it is from satisfying the PDE, its boundary values and its initial or terminal value. DGM \cite{sirignano2018dgm} is a close mesh-free relative and includes an American option among its tests. The deep BSDE solver \cite{han2018solving} aims at PDEs in many dimensions. In finance, PINN variants have priced contracts under Black-Scholes type equations \cite{bai2022application}, with early exercise \cite{gatta2023meshless} and under Heston dynamics \cite{hainaut2024option}. As far as we can tell, these papers measure price accuracy and do not report calibrated error bands.

before: \emph{Labelled learners and shape constraints.} Tree ensembles \cite{ho1995random,breiman2001random} and gradient boosting \cite{friedman2001greedy} are strong tabular regressors. Input-convex networks \cite{amos2017input} build convexity into the architecture, which matches the convexity of option prices in the underlying.
after: \emph{Learners trained on prices.} For tabular data, random forests \cite{ho1995random,breiman2001random} and boosted trees \cite{friedman2001greedy} are standard, well-tested choices. An input-convex network \cite{amos2017input} is convex in chosen inputs by design, and option prices are convex in the underlying.

before: \emph{Conformal prediction.} Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage under exchangeability \cite{vovk2005algorithmic}. The inductive or split version uses a held-out calibration set \cite{papadopoulos2002inductive}, and its regression guarantee is analysed in \cite{lei2018distribution}.
after: \emph{Distribution-free bands.} When the data are exchangeable, a conformal set contains the truth with a stated probability for any sample size \cite{vovk2005algorithmic}. A cheap variant fits the model once and sets the band width from residuals on points kept aside \cite{papadopoulos2002inductive}; Lei et al.~\cite{lei2018distribution} study what this variant guarantees for regression.

before: Normalised scores divide the residual by a local difficulty estimate \cite{papadopoulos2011regression}. Conformalized quantile regression \cite{romano2019conformalized} adapts width through quantile models, and Mondrian conformal regressors \cite{bostrom2020mondrian} calibrate inside categories. A tutorial is given in \cite{angelopoulos2023conformal}.
after: Scaling each residual by an estimate of local difficulty makes the band width vary from point to point \cite{papadopoulos2011regression}. CQR \cite{romano2019conformalized} gets a similar effect from quantile models. Mondrian regressors \cite{bostrom2020mondrian} repeat the calibration within each group of inputs. Angelopoulos and Bates \cite{angelopoulos2023conformal} give an accessible overview.
